question:
A cone has base radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm.

Work out the volume of the cone. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
solution:
Volume of a cone:
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$$

Substitute $r = 3$ and $h = 4$:
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 3^2 \times 4 = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 36 = 12\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

question:
A cone has base radius 6 cm and perpendicular height 4 cm.

Work out the volume of the cone. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hint: Only the radius has changed from a 3 cm radius cone. Substitute into $V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$, remembering to square the radius.
solution:
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 6^2 \times 4 = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 144 = 48\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

**What changed:** compared with a cone of radius 3 cm and height 4 cm (volume $12\pi$), the radius has doubled. Because the radius is squared, the volume is multiplied by $2^2 = 4$: $12\pi \times 4 = 48\pi$.

question:
A cone has base radius 6 cm and perpendicular height 8 cm.

Work out the volume of the cone. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hint: Compare with a cone of radius 6 cm and height 4 cm. Which feature has changed, and how does it affect the volume?
solution:
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 36 \times 8 = 96\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

**What changed:** compared with the cone of radius 6 cm and height 4 cm (volume $48\pi$), only the height has doubled. The height is not squared, so the volume just doubles: $48\pi \times 2 = 96\pi$.

question:
A cone has base radius 6 cm and **slant height** 10 cm.

Work out the volume of the cone. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
hint: The volume formula needs the perpendicular height, not the slant height. The radius, perpendicular height and slant height form a right-angled triangle.
solution:
**What changed:** this time we are given the slant height $l$, not the perpendicular height $h$.

The radius, perpendicular height and slant height form a right-angled triangle with $l$ as the hypotenuse:
$$h^2 + r^2 = l^2 \quad\Rightarrow\quad h = \sqrt{10^2 - 6^2} = \sqrt{64} = 8\text{ cm}$$

Now
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 36 \times 8 = 96\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

It is the same cone as the one with radius 6 cm and height 8 cm, just described differently. Using $l = 10$ in the volume formula would give the wrong answer $120\pi$.

question:
A sphere has radius 6 cm.

Work out
(a) the volume of the sphere,
(b) the surface area of the sphere.

Give each answer in terms of $\pi$ and also correct to 1 decimal place.
hint: $V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$ and $A = 4\pi r^2$. Cube the radius for volume, square it for area.
solution:
(a) $$V = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{4}{3} \times \pi \times 216 = 288\pi \approx 904.8\text{ cm}^3$$

(b) $$A = 4\pi r^2 = 4 \times \pi \times 36 = 144\pi \approx 452.4\text{ cm}^2$$

Note the units: volume is in $\text{cm}^3$, area in $\text{cm}^2$.

question:
The diagram shows a solid square-based pyramid. The base is a square of side 10 cm. The apex $V$ is vertically above the centre $M$ of the base, and the perpendicular height $VM$ is 12 cm.

(a) Work out the volume of the pyramid.
(b) Work out the total surface area of the pyramid.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><line x1="60" y1="250" x2="220" y2="250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="220" y1="250" x2="290" y2="195" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="290" y1="195" x2="130" y2="195" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="130" y1="195" x2="60" y2="250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="175" y1="45" x2="60" y2="250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="175" y1="45" x2="220" y2="250" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="175" y1="45" x2="290" y2="195" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="175" y1="45" x2="130" y2="195" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="175" y1="45" x2="175" y2="222.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="175,213.5 184,213.5 184,222.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><circle cx="175" cy="222.5" r="2.5" fill="currentColor"/><text x="140" y="274" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">10 cm</text><text x="269" y="238.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">10 cm</text><text x="175" y="37" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">V</text><text x="165" y="240.5" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">M</text></svg>
hint: For (b) you need the height of each triangular face (its slant height). Make a right-angled triangle from the perpendicular height and half the base side.
solution:
(a) $$V = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \text{base area} \times h = \tfrac{1}{3} \times 10^2 \times 12 = \tfrac{1}{3} \times 1200 = 400\text{ cm}^3$$

(b) Each triangular face has base 10 cm. Its height is the slant height $s$ from the apex to the midpoint of a base edge. The midpoint of a base edge is 5 cm from the centre of the base, so by Pythagoras:
$$s = \sqrt{12^2 + 5^2} = \sqrt{169} = 13\text{ cm}$$

Area of one triangular face:
$$\tfrac{1}{2} \times 10 \times 13 = 65\text{ cm}^2$$

Total surface area $=$ square base $+$ four triangles:
$$100 + 4 \times 65 = 360\text{ cm}^2$$

Using the perpendicular height 12 cm as the height of the triangles would give the wrong answer, 340 cm².

question:
Tom is asked to find the volume of a cone with base radius 4 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. His working is shown below.

$$V = \pi r^2 h = \pi \times 4^2 \times 9 = 144\pi \approx 452.4\text{ cm}^3$$

Identify Tom's mistake, explain why it is wrong, and work out the correct volume to 1 decimal place.
hint: Compare the formula Tom used with the formula for the volume of a cylinder.
answer: Tom used the cylinder formula and left out the $\frac{1}{3}$. Correct volume $= 48\pi \approx 150.8\text{ cm}^3$.
solution:
**Mistake:** Tom has used $V = \pi r^2 h$, which is the volume of a **cylinder**. The volume of a cone is
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$$

**Why:** a cone fills exactly one third of the cylinder with the same base and height (just as a pyramid is one third of the matching prism). Tom's answer is three times too big.

**Correct working:**
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 16 \times 9 = 48\pi \approx 150.8\text{ cm}^3$$

question:
A solid hemisphere has radius 5 cm. Aisha wants to find its total surface area so she can work out how much paint is needed to cover it completely. Her working is shown below.

Surface area of a sphere $= 4\pi r^2$.
A hemisphere is half a sphere, so surface area $= 2\pi r^2 = 2 \times \pi \times 25 = 50\pi \approx 157.1\text{ cm}^2$.

Identify Aisha's mistake, explain it, and give the correct total surface area to 1 decimal place.
hint: Imagine cutting a sphere in half. What new surface appears on each half?
answer: She forgot the flat circular face. Total surface area $= 3\pi r^2 = 75\pi \approx 235.6\text{ cm}^2$.
solution:
**Mistake:** $2\pi r^2$ is only the **curved** surface of the hemisphere. When a sphere is cut in half, each half also has a flat circular face of radius 5 cm, and the paint must cover that too.

**Correct working:**

Curved surface: $\tfrac{1}{2} \times 4\pi r^2 = 2\pi \times 25 = 50\pi$

Flat circle: $\pi r^2 = 25\pi$

$$\text{Total} = 50\pi + 25\pi = 75\pi \approx 235.6\text{ cm}^2$$

In general a solid hemisphere has total surface area $3\pi r^2$.

question:
The diagram shows a frustum. Its base has radius 9 cm, its top has radius 3 cm and its perpendicular height is 12 cm. The top and base are parallel circles.

Leo works out the volume like this:

$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi (9 - 3)^2 \times 12 = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 36 \times 12 = 144\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

(a) Explain what is wrong with Leo's method.
(b) Work out the correct volume of the frustum. Give your answer in terms of $\pi$.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><path d="M45 245 A135 22 0 0 0 315 245" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M45 245 A135 22 0 0 1 315 245" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><ellipse cx="180" cy="65" rx="45" ry="8" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="45" y1="245" x2="135" y2="65" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="315" y1="245" x2="225" y2="65" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="180" y1="65" x2="180" y2="245" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><polyline points="180,237 188,237 188,245" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" fill="none"/><line x1="180" y1="65" x2="225" y2="65" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><line x1="180" y1="245" x2="315" y2="245" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="202.5" y="53" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">3 cm</text><text x="257.5" y="285" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">9 cm</text><text x="174" y="155" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">12 cm</text></svg>
hint: Extend the sloping sides until they meet. The frustum is a large cone with a small cone removed. Use similar triangles to find the height of the small cone.
answer: (a) A frustum is not a cone with radius $9 - 3$; it is a large cone minus a small similar cone. (b) $468\pi\text{ cm}^3$ ($\approx 1470.3\text{ cm}^3$)
solution:
(a) Leo has treated the frustum as a single cone of radius $9 - 3 = 6$ cm. Subtracting the radii does not give any part of the solid. A frustum is what is left when a small cone is cut off the top of a large cone, so its volume is **large cone $-$ small cone**.

(b) Complete the cone. The small cone (removed) and the large cone are similar. Let the small cone have height $x$. Comparing radius to height:
$$\frac{3}{x} = \frac{9}{x + 12} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 9x = 3x + 36 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 6\text{ cm}$$

So the large cone has radius 9 cm and height $6 + 12 = 18$ cm, and the small cone has radius 3 cm and height 6 cm.

$$V_{\text{large}} = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 81 \times 18 = 486\pi$$
$$V_{\text{small}} = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 9 \times 6 = 18\pi$$
$$V_{\text{frustum}} = 486\pi - 18\pi = 468\pi \approx 1470.3\text{ cm}^3$$

question:
An ice-cream shop fills a cone completely with ice cream and then puts a hemisphere of ice cream on top, as shown. The cone has radius 3 cm and perpendicular height 11 cm. The hemisphere has radius 3 cm.

(a) Work out the volume of ice cream in one serving. Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
(b) The shop has a full 5 litre tub of ice cream. How many complete servings can be made from the tub? ($1\text{ litre} = 1000\text{ cm}^3$)
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><path d="M132 92 A48 48 0 0 1 228 92" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M132 92 A48 10 0 0 0 228 92" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M132 92 A48 10 0 0 1 228 92" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="132" y1="92" x2="180" y2="268" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="228" y1="92" x2="180" y2="268" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="180" y1="92" x2="228" y2="92" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="204" y="77" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">3 cm</text><line x1="180" y1="92" x2="180" y2="268" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="262" y1="92" x2="262" y2="268" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="256" y1="92" x2="268" y2="92" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="256" y1="268" x2="268" y2="268" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="270" y="185" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">11 cm</text></svg>
hint: Add the volume of the cone, $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h$, to the volume of the hemisphere, $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$. Then convert 5 litres to $\text{cm}^3$.
solution:
(a) Cone:
$$\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 9 \times 11 = 33\pi$$

Hemisphere (half of $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$):
$$\tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3 = \tfrac{2}{3} \times \pi \times 27 = 18\pi$$

Total:
$$33\pi + 18\pi = 51\pi \approx 160.2\text{ cm}^3$$

(b) $5\text{ litres} = 5000\text{ cm}^3$.
$$5000 \div 160.22\ldots = 31.2\ldots$$

Only complete servings count, so round **down**: **31 servings**.

question:
A cylinder, a cone and a sphere all have radius $r$. The cylinder and the cone both have height $2r$, so the sphere fits exactly inside the cylinder.

Show that the volumes of the cone, the sphere and the cylinder are in the ratio $1 : 2 : 3$.
hint: Write each volume in terms of $r$ by replacing $h$ with $2r$. Then divide each by the smallest.
answer: Cone $= \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$, sphere $= \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$, cylinder $= 2\pi r^3 = \frac{6}{3}\pi r^3$, so the ratio is $2 : 4 : 6 = 1 : 2 : 3$.
solution:
Use $h = 2r$ in each formula.

Cone:
$$\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 (2r) = \tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3$$

Sphere:
$$\tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3$$

Cylinder:
$$\pi r^2 (2r) = 2\pi r^3 = \tfrac{6}{3}\pi r^3$$

So
$$\text{cone} : \text{sphere} : \text{cylinder} = \tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3 : \tfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 : \tfrac{6}{3}\pi r^3 = 2 : 4 : 6 = 1 : 2 : 3$$

This holds for **every** value of $r$, because $r^3$ and $\pi$ cancel. (Archimedes was so proud of this result that he asked for a sphere inside a cylinder to be carved on his tombstone.) It also shows that sphere $=$ cylinder $-$ cone.

question:
Cone P is a right cone. Cone Q is an oblique cone: its apex is not directly above the centre of its base. Both cones have base radius 4 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. The diagram also shows a horizontal cross-section of each cone 3 cm above the base.

Kai says, "Cone Q has a longer sloping side, so it must hold more."

(a) Use Cavalieri's principle to explain why Kai is wrong.
(b) Work out the volume of cone Q, correct to 1 decimal place.

hint: Cavalieri's principle: two solids of equal height whose cross-sections at every level have equal areas have equal volumes. Compare the cross-sections of P and Q at the same height.
answer: (a) At every height the cross-sections of P and Q are circles of the same radius, so (Cavalieri) the volumes are equal. (b) $48\pi \approx 150.8\text{ cm}^3$
solution:
(a) Both cones have the same height, 9 cm. Slice both cones horizontally at the same height $y$ above the base. In each cone the slice is a circle, an enlargement of the base from the apex with scale factor $\frac{9 - y}{9}$, so its radius is
$$4 \times \frac{9 - y}{9}$$
in **both** cones (the slant of Q only shifts the circle sideways). For example, 3 cm above the base both cross-sections are circles of radius $4 \times \frac{6}{9} = \frac{8}{3}$ cm.

Since the cross-sections have equal area at every level and the heights are equal, Cavalieri's principle says the volumes are equal. A longer sloping side does not mean a bigger volume.

(b) So Q has the same volume as the right cone P:
$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \tfrac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 16 \times 9 = 48\pi \approx 150.8\text{ cm}^3$$

Note that $h$ must be the **perpendicular** height, not the length of the sloping side.

question: A toy is made from a solid cone on top of a solid hemisphere, as shown. The cone and the hemisphere both have radius 4 cm. The total height of the toy is 13 cm.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><line x1="114" y1="176" x2="170" y2="50" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="226" y1="176" x2="170" y2="50" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M114 176 A56 11 0 0 0 226 176" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M114 176 A56 11 0 0 1 226 176" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><path d="M114 176 A56 56 0 0 0 226 176" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><line x1="170" y1="176" x2="226" y2="176" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="198" y="161" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">4 cm</text><line x1="270" y1="50" x2="270" y2="232" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="264" y1="50" x2="276" y2="50" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="264" y1="232" x2="276" y2="232" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="278" y="146" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="start">13 cm</text></svg>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Show that the slant height of the cone is $\sqrt{97}$ cm.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Work out the volume of the toy. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Work out the total surface area of the toy. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

hint: The hemisphere's height equals its radius, so the cone's perpendicular height is $13 - 4$. The outside of the toy is the curved surface of the cone plus the curved surface of the hemisphere only.
solution:
(a) The hemisphere has height equal to its radius, 4 cm, so the cone's perpendicular height is
$$h = 13 - 4 = 9\text{ cm} \quad \text{(M1)}$$
$$l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2} = \sqrt{16 + 81} = \sqrt{97}\text{ cm} \quad \text{(A1)}$$

(b) $$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 4^2 \times 9 + \tfrac{2}{3}\pi \times 4^3 = 48\pi + \tfrac{128}{3}\pi \quad \text{(M1)}$$
$$= \tfrac{272}{3}\pi = 284.83\ldots \approx 285\text{ cm}^3 \quad \text{(A1)}$$

(c) The flat faces are joined together, so they are **not** on the outside. Surface $=$ curved surface of cone $+$ curved surface of hemisphere.

Cone: $\pi r l = 4\sqrt{97}\,\pi = 123.76\ldots$ (M1, using the slant height)

Hemisphere: $2\pi r^2 = 32\pi = 100.53\ldots$ (M1)

$$\text{Total} = 224.29\ldots \approx 224\text{ cm}^2 \quad \text{(A1)}$$

question:
A cone has volume $144\pi\text{ cm}^3$. Its perpendicular height is twice its base radius.

Work out the exact curved surface area of the cone. Give your answer in the form $k\sqrt{5}\,\pi\text{ cm}^2$, where $k$ is an integer. Do not use a calculator.
hint: Let the radius be $r$, so $h = 2r$. Form an equation for the volume in terms of $r$ and solve it. Then find the slant height as a surd.
solution:
Let the radius be $r$, so $h = 2r$.
$$\tfrac{1}{3}\pi r^2 (2r) = 144\pi \quad\Rightarrow\quad \tfrac{2}{3} r^3 = 144 \quad\Rightarrow\quad r^3 = 216 \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = 6$$

So $r = 6$ cm and $h = 12$ cm.

Slant height by Pythagoras:
$$l = \sqrt{6^2 + 12^2} = \sqrt{180} = \sqrt{36 \times 5} = 6\sqrt{5}\text{ cm}$$

Curved surface area:
$$\pi r l = \pi \times 6 \times 6\sqrt{5} = 36\sqrt{5}\,\pi\text{ cm}^2$$

So $k = 36$.

question:
A paperweight is a solid steel hemisphere. Its mass is 1 kg. The density of steel is $7.8\text{ g/cm}^3$.

(a) Work out the radius of the hemisphere. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
(b) The whole paperweight, including its flat base, is to be coated in a thin layer of lacquer. Work out the total area to be coated, correct to 3 significant figures.
hint: Volume $=$ mass $\div$ density (use grams). The volume of a hemisphere is $\frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$. For (b), remember the flat face.
solution:
(a) Mass $= 1\text{ kg} = 1000\text{ g}$.
$$\text{Volume} = \frac{\text{mass}}{\text{density}} = \frac{1000}{7.8} = 128.205\ldots\text{ cm}^3$$

Set this equal to the hemisphere volume:
$$\tfrac{2}{3}\pi r^3 = 128.205\ldots \quad\Rightarrow\quad r^3 = \frac{3 \times 128.205\ldots}{2\pi} = 61.21\ldots$$
$$r = \sqrt[3]{61.21\ldots} = 3.9410\ldots \approx 3.94\text{ cm}$$

(b) Total surface area of a solid hemisphere $=$ curved surface $2\pi r^2$ $+$ flat circle $\pi r^2$ $= 3\pi r^2$:
$$3\pi \times 3.9410\ldots^2 = 146.38\ldots \approx 146\text{ cm}^2$$

(Use the unrounded radius; using only $2\pi r^2$ would miss the base.)

question:
A hollow cone has base radius 6 cm and perpendicular height 8 cm. A sphere is placed inside so that it touches the base of the cone and touches the curved surface all the way round.

(a) Find the radius of the sphere.
(b) What fraction of the volume of the cone does the sphere occupy?
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><path d="M60 255 A120 22 0 0 0 300 255" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M60 255 A120 22 0 0 1 300 255" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="60" y1="255" x2="180" y2="95" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="255" x2="180" y2="95" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="180" cy="195" r="60" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="#3b82f6" fill-opacity="0.2"/><line x1="180" y1="95" x2="180" y2="255" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="180" y1="255" x2="60" y2="255" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"/><text x="116" y="249" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">6 cm</text><line x1="322" y1="95" x2="322" y2="255" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="316" y1="95" x2="328" y2="95" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="316" y1="255" x2="328" y2="255" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="318" y="180" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">8 cm</text></svg>
hint: Take a vertical cross-section through the apex: an isosceles triangle with a circle touching all three sides. The radius from the centre to a sloping side is perpendicular to it, giving a pair of similar right-angled triangles.
solution:
(a) A vertical cross-section through the apex $A$ is an isosceles triangle with base 12 cm and height 8 cm. The slant side is $\sqrt{6^2 + 8^2} = 10$ cm. The sphere appears as a circle of radius $r$ touching all three sides, with centre $O$ on the axis, $r$ above the base. So $AO = 8 - r$.

Let $T$ be where the circle touches a sloping side. $OT = r$ and $OT$ is perpendicular to the side, so triangle $ATO$ is right-angled at $T$. It is similar to the triangle formed by the apex, the centre of the base and a base edge point (they share the angle at $A$):
$$\frac{OT}{AO} = \frac{6}{10} \quad\Rightarrow\quad \frac{r}{8 - r} = \frac{3}{5} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 5r = 24 - 3r \quad\Rightarrow\quad r = 3\text{ cm}$$

(Check with area $=$ $r \times$ semi-perimeter: the triangle has area $\frac{1}{2} \times 12 \times 8 = 48$ and semi-perimeter $\frac{10 + 10 + 12}{2} = 16$, so $r = \frac{48}{16} = 3$.)

(b) $$V_{\text{sphere}} = \tfrac{4}{3}\pi \times 3^3 = 36\pi, \qquad V_{\text{cone}} = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 6^2 \times 8 = 96\pi$$
$$\text{Fraction} = \frac{36\pi}{96\pi} = \frac{3}{8}$$

question:
A plastic bucket is in the shape of a frustum of a cone, as shown. The top is a circle of diameter 30 cm, the bottom is a circle of diameter 20 cm and the depth of the bucket is 24 cm.

(a) Work out the capacity of the bucket in litres, correct to 1 decimal place. ($1\text{ litre} = 1000\text{ cm}^3$)
(b) Mia fills the empty bucket using a 2-litre jug. How many times must she fill the jug to fill the bucket to the top?
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><ellipse cx="180" cy="52" rx="120" ry="18" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M100 244 A80 12 0 0 0 260 244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M100 244 A80 12 0 0 1 260 244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="60" y1="52" x2="100" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="52" x2="260" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="52" x2="300" y2="52" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="180" y="28" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">30 cm</text><line x1="100" y1="244" x2="260" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="180" y="274" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">20 cm</text><line x1="330" y1="52" x2="330" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="324" y1="52" x2="336" y2="52" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="324" y1="244" x2="336" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="326" y="153" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">24 cm</text></svg>
hint: Extend the bucket's sides down to a point to make a complete (upside-down) cone. Use similar triangles with the radii 10 cm and 15 cm to find the height of the small cone that has been removed.
solution:
(a) The radii are 15 cm (top) and 10 cm (bottom). Extend the sides to meet at a point below the bucket. Let the small cone (the missing tip) have height $x$. By similar triangles:
$$\frac{10}{x} = \frac{15}{x + 24} \quad\Rightarrow\quad 15x = 10x + 240 \quad\Rightarrow\quad x = 48\text{ cm}$$

So the full cone has radius 15 cm and height $48 + 24 = 72$ cm.

$$V = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 15^2 \times 72 - \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 10^2 \times 48 = 5400\pi - 1600\pi = 3800\pi\text{ cm}^3$$
$$3800\pi = 11\,938.0\ldots\text{ cm}^3 \approx 11.9\text{ litres}$$

(b) $11.938 \div 2 = 5.97\ldots$. Five jugs (10 litres) are not enough, so Mia must fill the jug **6 times** (the last jug is not completely emptied).

question:
The empty bucket from the diagram (a frustum with top diameter 30 cm, bottom diameter 20 cm and depth 24 cm, capacity $3800\pi\text{ cm}^3$) is filled with water to a depth of 12 cm.

Ben says, "The water is half the depth of the bucket, so the bucket is half full."

Show that Ben is wrong, and find the percentage of the bucket's capacity that is filled, correct to the nearest 1%.
diagram: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 360 290" width="360" height="290"><ellipse cx="180" cy="52" rx="120" ry="18" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M100 244 A80 12 0 0 0 260 244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none"/><path d="M100 244 A80 12 0 0 1 260 244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="60" y1="52" x2="100" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="300" y1="52" x2="260" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="60" y1="52" x2="300" y2="52" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="180" y="28" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">30 cm</text><line x1="100" y1="244" x2="260" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><text x="180" y="274" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="middle">20 cm</text><line x1="330" y1="52" x2="330" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="324" y1="52" x2="336" y2="52" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><line x1="324" y1="244" x2="336" y2="244" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1"/><text x="326" y="153" fill="currentColor" font-size="14" font-family="sans-serif" text-anchor="end">24 cm</text></svg>
hint: The bucket gets wider as you go up, so the top half holds more than the bottom half. Find the radius of the water surface (it is halfway between 10 cm and 15 cm), then treat the water as a frustum too.
answer: Water volume $= 1525\pi\text{ cm}^3$, which is $\frac{61}{152} \approx 40\%$ of the capacity, not 50%.
solution:
The radius increases steadily (linearly) with height from 10 cm at the bottom to 15 cm at the top, so at a depth of 12 cm (halfway up) the water surface has radius 12.5 cm.

Use the completed cone from the bucket: the missing tip below the base has height 48 cm and radius 10 cm. The water surface is $48 + 12 = 60$ cm above the apex. (Check by similarity: $\frac{12.5}{60} = \frac{10}{48}$.)

$$V_{\text{water}} = \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 12.5^2 \times 60 - \tfrac{1}{3}\pi \times 10^2 \times 48 = 3125\pi - 1600\pi = 1525\pi\text{ cm}^3$$

Fraction of capacity:
$$\frac{1525\pi}{3800\pi} = \frac{61}{152} = 0.401\ldots \approx 40\%$$

So the bucket is only about 40% full, not 50%. Ben is wrong because the bucket is narrower at the bottom: the lower half of the depth holds less than the upper half. (Halving the depth does not halve the volume of a frustum, just as subtracting dimensions does not give its volume.)
